summary: A response to claims in several mail and FTP RFCs that network mail should be free, meaning that no login should be required. Padlipsky argues that free does not have to mean login-less: explicit login to a free account could be more natural on some systems. It is a discussion of a design choice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 491 argues that free mail does not have to mean mail without a login. It proposes the same free account name on every host so users would not need a different login for each system.

questions: what is free in network mail
subtitle: A proposal for making network mail free without requiring a different login at each host.

tldr.problem: Several mail-related RFCs equated free network mail with not requiring a login, but some host systems may work more naturally with an explicit login.
tldr.mechanism: Padlipsky proposes a shared free-mail login, USER NETML and PASS NETML, and suggests a FREE command if some hosts cannot accept that approach.
tldr.outcome: RFC 491 argues for a design choice and does not specify an adopted protocol.

today: The unit records RFC 491's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It is a position paper on how FTP might handle free network mail.

sections.title: Free Mail and Login
sections.content:
Padlipsky responds to statements in RFCs 454, 475 and 479 that network mail should be free, meaning no login or USER command is needed. He argues that “free” does not require a loginless method: users could explicitly log in to a free account.

Some host systems may find explicit login more natural. The proposal is that a free account have the same name on every host, so users do not have to remember a separate name for each system.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail can be free even if the user signs in. The author proposes using one shared account name on every host.

sections.title: The NETML Login Proposal
sections.content:
The suggested login is USER NETML followed by PASS NETML. The author says the name is short and uppercase so it should fit the least common denominator of user identifiers, and is unlikely to conflict with a person's initials.

If some hosts object to NETML, Padlipsky proposes adding an FTP FREE command. This would let a server provide free mail without treating the MAIL command itself as an implicit login.
sections.plainLanguage: NETML is a proposed common name for a free-mail account. A separate FREE command is offered as an alternative for hosts that cannot use it.

sections.title: Login Can Identify the User
sections.content:
The author argues that login can serve authentication as well as accounting. On systems that control mailbox access, a process's principal identifier is associated with it at login and must match an entry on the mailbox's access-control list.

He questions whether a separate command such as the FROM command discussed in RFC 475 is needed to identify a sender. He also says that making MAIL imply login could create implementation difficulties and that the FTP discussion of login requirements is internally inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: On some systems, login tells the computer who is asking to use a mailbox. The author says a separate sender-identification mechanism may duplicate that role.

references.text: RFCs 454, 475 and 479, cited in the discussion of free network mail.
